item.title: This artificial artificial artificial intelligence.
item.description:
In the early 1780s, wealthy Parisians sent their laundry across the Atlantic to be washed in Haiti. The reason was that, beyond the high cost of local services, French laundry after washing frankly turned yellow, whereas laundry brought back from Saint-Domingue—where the equatorial sun combined with local indigo produced a bluish whiteness unattainable in Europe—attracted attention and signaled the owner's status.

It’s amusing how the outsourcing model to exotic countries still works today: text annotation for popular LLMs is given to cheap labor from, say, Nigeria. But since cheap labor is usually also cunning, manual text annotation services like "Mechanical Turk" have faced the issue that between 30% and 50% of workers themselves started running tasks through free Chinese neural networks. As a result, in early July 2026, Amazon posted a banner on the Mechanical Turk website stating they were no longer accepting new clients, marking the end of a mini-era. Even more ironic is that the platform operated for 21 years under the unofficial slogan "Artificial Artificial Intelligence." And, apparently, the time has come for yet another level of abstraction.

Read more

item.title: XSIM: How We Reinvented Splatting for Simulation of Autonomous Vehicle Sensors
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Dmitry Senyushkin, this is AIRI and the “Autonomous Vision” team. Our research group is actively interested in the topic of self-driving cars, and today we would like to talk about one of our latest developments in the field of simulation for testing and training algorithms.

In this field, not only the volume of training data plays an important role, but also its diversity. This problem can be solved with the help of synthetic data produced by realistic road simulators. We followed this path and created XSIM — a new technology that required rethinking traditional object representation pipelines. We presented XSIM at the recently held IJCAI 2026, and here I will summarize the essence of our work.

item.title: Building agents on A2A with isolated execution in Go: running an AI developer in the cloud while maintaining control
item.description:
My name is Vera Kasyanenko, I am a developer from the DevRails AI team at MTS Web Services. We are currently building an agent-developer — a service where the language model itself writes code, runs tests, performs reviews, and creates commits.

When you integrate the model into a service and provide it with tools, an inconvenient fact quickly becomes apparent: the commands it generates are executed somewhere. And the answer to the question of where exactly — and who manages that location — determines the entire remaining architecture.

In this article, we will examine three possible schemes: from the least isolated to the platform-based one, and analyze how each is structured, where it breaks down, and which one we ended up with.

Read more

item.title: Teaching AI to prepare datasets for the Bitrix24 BI constructor

item.title: How to maintain a large knowledge base for RAG and update it in a semi-automatic mode
item.description:
A large knowledge base has an unpleasant property. It answers well the questions that have been put into it, but gives no indication of questions that are missing.

A user asks a question to an AI agent, RAG does not find suitable material, and the dialogue is escalated to a specialist. The operator investigates and writes the correct answer. A few days later, another user comes with the same problem, but nothing has changed for the Agent. The answer already exists within the company, it just remains in the support history.

The more inquiries, the worse the manual loop works. The product manager sees the overall handoff rate to the operator, the editor receives individual requests to update the knowledge base, and recurring questions get lost among thousands of dialogues. As a result, RAG is updated based on gut feelings, loud complaints, and randomly noticed cases.

We decided to build a service that automatically finds such gaps. It reads inquiries, extracts useful operator responses, merges duplicates, compares the result with the current knowledge base, and prepares recommendations for the editor.

Read more

item.title: 6 new neural network training methods that were invented millennia ago
item.description:
Neural networks in their modern form have been around for several decades. But humanity has been grappling with the question "how does knowledge even arise?" for over two thousand years. So, I reasoned, somewhere between Plato, Aristotle, Peirce, Hegel, and Kant, there must surely lie a forgotten learning method. All that's left is to translate it from philosophical language into PyTorch and call backward().

The plan was excellent. I took a list of machine learning methods, mapped it onto philosophical theories of knowledge, and initially got twelve "unused" ideas. Then I started checking the literature — and half the list disappeared.

Peirce's abduction already lives in Abductive Learning and neuro-symbolic systems. Skeptical suspension of judgment is called selective prediction. Embodied cognition rides around laboratories in robots. Teleology has settled into goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Even dialectics has already reached individual algorithmic works.

So, there was no free optimization to be found with Plato, and what I did find, I've packaged here: https://github.com/webzuweb/philosophia_torch

However, something more useful was discovered: philosophy more often gives machine learning not ready-made algorithms, but problem formulations. "What does it mean to know the limits of one's knowledge?", "how to understand the part through the whole?", "how to preserve both poles of a contradiction?", "what remains if you temporarily disable a habitual premise?" — these are almost technical specifications. What's missing is the state, the operator, the loss function, and the experiment in which the idea can fail.

In this article, I will divide philosophical analogies into three classes, then analyze six mechanisms that are still only partially formalized, and present a unified PyTorch module. Unlike the first version, this one includes not only formulas and tests, but also two reproducible synthetic experiments.

Read more

item.title: [Translation] Process discipline is boring. That’s exactly why agents need it.
item.description:
After several successful pilot projects with agents, many organizations are quietly starting to notice that the efficiency gains are somehow leaking away. Disparate agents create duplicate work, conflicts, and edge cases that no one is responsible for. Talking to clients, I realized I've seen this movie before.

Every technological wave has a question that seems obvious in hindsight but gets overlooked in the midst of widespread enthusiasm. For microservices, that question was: who actually owns the end‑to‑end flow of a customer scenario? For agents, I think the question is the same.

The promise of microservices was that development teams could stay independent and move faster — services would simply react to events, without any need for coordination. At first, it even worked. Adding a new service was easy: you just started consuming events from an existing system, without having to talk to any event producer. Teams moved fast.

The dominant coordination style was called choreography: services don't communicate with each other directly. Instead, they generate events (e.g., order placed, payment confirmed, item reserved), and other services react to those events independently. This way, no central coordinator is needed, and maybe you don't even need to define an explicit sequence. Each service minds its own business, resulting in a loosely coupled architecture (spoiler: it wasn't loosely coupled — as I broke down in a talk titled "Loose or Crappy Coupling? Understanding Communication Patterns in Microservice Architectures").

Read more

item.title: Three negative AI responses turned out to be about another company: analysis of one error in the sentiment metric.
item.description:
I decided to count how many times language models respond negatively about a specific company. It seemed like a simple task: run queries through several models, label the sentiment of the responses, and divide the negative ones by the total number. I got three negative responses out of 358 — 0.8%. The number looked harmless, and I almost submitted it as is in the report.

Then I opened those three responses to understand why exactly the model gave a negative rating. Same model, same query, three consecutive runs. And the sentiment was negative not about the company I was measuring, but about a namesake with a similar name — a completely different business.

This made me recalculate everything from scratch and discover that the negative share as a metric has at least three points where it silently lies: an incorrect denominator, a lack of verification that the model is actually talking about your company, and model refusals that fall into neither of the two categories.

Read more

item.title: Not another chatbot: how AI agents are embedded into corporate processes
item.description:
Corporate AI is gradually moving beyond the dialog window. For a language model to bring value to a business, it is not enough to be able to answer questions. It must obtain authorized data from information systems, operate according to a given scenario, and deliver a result that employees can use in a specific process.

This approach underlies the AI agent platform being developed by Infostart. Its key idea is not to create a universal digital assistant, but rather individual agents with specific roles, data sources, rules, and output formats…

Read more

item.title: Gigawatts on Paper: The AI Boom Hits Not the Chips, but the Socket
item.description:
According to the forecast of the International Energy Agency (IEA), by 2030, data centers, AI, and cryptocurrencies are expected to consume a total of about 945 TWh per year — as much as all of Japan currently consumes. The crux of this statement lies in the word "expected." No matter how beautiful the dream of AGI may be, everything ultimately and reductively boils down to a mundane problem — the availability of electricity. But if big techs promise in press releases to open huge ten-gigawatt plants, then there are no power supply issues — right? Right?

Well, let's check.

item.title: AI agent instead of a tester: 20 kopecks per dialogue and the reason why an LLM won't replace you
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Nikita Khrobostov, and I am a QA engineer at Just AI. I test dialog systems: chatbots and voice bots, some of which involve RAG queries.

My work is structured like this: I take a dialog schema on Canvas, put myself in the client's shoes, and go through the scenario step by step. I ask a question and check the response; if I agree, I see if the transition works correctly; if I refuse, I check the fallback. This means I have to go through dozens of scenarios, which in a large project quickly add up to a significant amount of manual work.

To give you an idea of the scale. In our voice bot project, we have 13 active scenarios; in the chatbot, just one. To fully test a single scenario, it takes anywhere from 40 to over a hundred calls, and the number of test cases is two to four times larger, depending on the design. A full check of one small scenario takes 5–6 hours.

The problem isn't so much the number of tests, but that a person running through the fiftieth test case in a day starts to sound like an automaton: using short, templated phrases, because they're focused on coverage rather than natural speech. But a real user speaks very differently. It's precisely with natural speech that the NLU part breaks down, and these are the bugs that are easiest to miss.

The idea of automating this work with an AI agent has been around for a while. I'll tell you how I approached it twice. The second time, I put together a working prototype in one day that is already finding bugs. The material turned out to be as sincere and honest as possible: with numbers, with failures, and with places where the solution is still unfinished.

Read more

item.title: I am conducting a test drive of GigaChat Audio under working conditions.
item.description:
Hello, Habr! Sber recently released a new model, GigaChat Audio. Right now I'm dictating this text to the model with my voice — the final touch in the story of how I put it through its test drive.

When I read that GigaChat Audio remembers context, navigates large audio recordings, and even senses the speaker's emotions, I immediately wanted to test it. I deployed this model locally on my work computer and spent the whole day evaluating it on actual work tasks. The result is in this article.

My name is Danila @pushnoydan, I'm a mid‑level developer working on microservice backend. At the same time, I'm a big enthusiast of AI models: in my free time I dig into them to better understand the capabilities of new releases, and I try to apply them at work to simplify routine tasks.

GigaChat Audio is an audio‑native LLM. Over the course of the day, I tasked it with parsing voice communications from colleagues, creating summaries of audio recordings, and extracting key context from recordings of various meetings. Let's see how the model performed on real‑world tasks.

Read more
